title: Unsupervised Event Coreference Resolution with Rich Linguistic Features
abstract: Applies nonparametric Bayesian clustering with rich linguistic features to open-domain event coreference. The evaluation explicitly covers both within-document and cross-document event coreference, making the work relevant to evidence combination for same-event clustering.

admission.reason: The abstract establishes cross-document event-coreference relevance, but only characterizes the evidence as 'rich linguistic features' and does not identify which evidence combinations materially establish or reject identity. Stronger candidates in this set provide explicit analyses of argument evidence, context, discourse structure, or same-versus-different hypotheses, so this paper has insufficient marginal value for the limited reading round.

title: Enhancing Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution by Discourse Structure and Semantic Information
abstract: Augments cross-document event-coreference evidence with rhetorical document structure and cross-document lexical chains, while noting that argument features such as location, time, agent, and patient are commonly used evidence. It evaluates same-event clustering on English data and a newly constructed Chinese cross-document event-coreference dataset.

admission.reason: The paper is genuinely about cross-document event coreference, but its stated contribution overlaps heavily with stronger admitted F1 evidence on discourse/context and event arguments. The abstract does not show a distinctive analysis of which individual evidence combinations establish versus refute identity, so the marginal reading value is insufficient. Its identifier is also UNCHECKED.

title: Harvesting Events from Multiple Sources: Towards a Cross-Document Event Extraction Paradigm
abstract: Defines a cross-document event-extraction pipeline that explicitly includes event coreference resolution before normalization and entity-role resolution, allowing information about one event to be integrated across sources. It introduces the CLES dataset with cross-document events and evaluates the complete pipeline, making it relevant as adjacent evidence for multi-source event identity.

admission.reason: The abstract confirms a multi-source extraction pipeline containing event coreference, but it does not establish whether the coreference component is separately evaluated or whether the paper analyzes evidence for same-event identity rather than only end-to-end extraction quality. Admit only if the full paper reports standalone cross-document identity evaluation, error analysis, or evidence ablations that materially inform F1 or F10.

title: Multimodal Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution Using Linear Semantic Transfer and Mixed-Modality Ensembles
abstract: Studies whether distinct event mentions in a multi-document corpus refer to the same underlying occurrence and tests visual evidence in addition to text. It augments ECB+ with event-centric images and evaluates multimodal fusion, cross-modal linear mapping, and mixed-modality ensembles on ECB+ and AIDA Phase 1.

admission.reason: This is valid direct cross-document event-coreference work, but the distinctive contribution is multimodal image evidence. That modality is peripheral to the current Outlook/Teams work-matter identity problem, while several admitted F1 papers address more transferable textual, argument, discourse, and robustness evidence. The verified identity does not outweigh the lower project-specific marginal value.

title: Text Classification and Named Entities for New Event Detection
abstract: Investigates new-event detection using text classification and named-entity information and develops a multistage system that improves over single-stage baselines. Its experiments show that named entities are useful only in some circumstances rather than constituting sufficient event-identity evidence by themselves.

admission.reason: The abstract is relevant to F3 and usefully notes that named entities are not universally sufficient, but this contribution is substantially covered by the admitted new-event papers, especially the candidate that explicitly separates names, topics, and full-text similarities. With scarce reading slots, this does not add enough beyond that evidence decomposition. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

title: Learning approaches for detecting and tracking news events
abstract: Adapts information-retrieval and machine-learning methods to detecting novel events in chronologically ordered news streams and tracking already identified events over time. The task structure provides transferable evidence for distinguishing new event identity from continuation.
venue: IEEE Intelligent Systems and their Applications

admission.reason: The abstract establishes the standard detect-and-track news-event capability but does not identify a distinctive mechanism, evidence analysis, uncertainty treatment, or incremental behavior beyond what is already supplied by the stronger admitted F3 candidates. It therefore duplicates the transfer capability without materially strengthening the stream. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

title: Identity, non-identity, and near-identity: Addressing the complexity of coreference
abstract: Argues that reference identity is not always adequately modeled as a simple binary relation and develops a continuum from full identity through near-identity to non-identity. It discusses granularity, individuation, and identity criteria, providing transferable semantics for distinguishing strict continuation from related but non-identical instances.

admission.reason: The continuum from identity through near-identity to non-identity is conceptually relevant, but the abstract is general coreference semantics rather than event-specific or workplace identity. The admitted subevent paper provides much more direct evidence for the concrete partial-event distinction needed here, so this broader linguistic treatment does not justify an additional reading slot. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

title: Linear Cross-document Event Coreference Resolution with X-AMR
abstract: Represents individual event mentions with cross-document AMR graphs and uses a multi-hop algorithm to linearize event-coreference decisions that otherwise require pairwise comparisons. The work also uses the representation to assess LLM event-coreference judgments against human annotations.

admission.reason: The paper is clearly in F1, but the abstract emphasizes X-AMR representation, multi-hop linearization of pairwise decisions, and assessment of LLM judgments. It does not show a distinctive analysis of identity evidence or partial/evolving relations, and its contribution is more about representation and computational organization than the current open gaps. Stronger verified and unverified F1 candidates are admitted.

title: Synergetic Event Understanding: A Collaborative Approach to Cross-Document Event Coreference Resolution with Large Language Models
abstract: Addresses clustering event mentions across documents that refer to the same real-world event. An LLM first produces richer event understanding and summaries, while a task-specific smaller model learns refined event representations; the approach is evaluated across multiple cross-document event-coreference datasets.

admission.reason: The abstract demonstrates another capable cross-document event-coreference architecture, but its main contribution is LLM-assisted event understanding and representation learning. It does not expose which evidence establishes or refutes identity, how uncertainty is handled, or how partial identity is distinguished, so it adds little to the specific gaps relative to the admitted F1 papers.

title: Employing Discourse Coherence Enhancement to Improve Cross-Document Event and Entity Coreference Resolution
abstract: Introduces Cross-Document Discourse Coherence Enhancement to create coherent context between mentions that originate in separate documents. The generated coherent text is then used to represent mentions and resolve cross-document event or entity coreference.

admission.reason: Creating coherent cross-document context is relevant, but this capability substantially overlaps the admitted discourse/context paper and the separate 2025 coherence-and-structure candidate. The abstract does not show a unique evidence analysis, work-domain result, or identity-relation distinction sufficient to justify another slot. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

title: Position-aware end-to-end cross-document event coreference resolution for Dutch
abstract: Presents an end-to-end cross-document event-coreference system combining positional knowledge and graph representations. It is evaluated on a large Dutch event-coreference dataset and includes qualitative and quantitative analysis of errors in predicted coreference chains.

admission.reason: The end-to-end Dutch CDCR system and error analysis are relevant to F1, but the abstract does not identify a distinctive identity-evidence result beyond positional and graph modeling. Language coverage and generic chain-error analysis alone do not close the present gaps, and stronger papers already cover evidence composition and robustness. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

title: Lifelong Learning Augmented Short Text Stream Clustering Method
abstract: Introduces a one-pass short-text stream clustering method augmented with episodic memory and sparse experience replay. Periodic replay of recent observations updates cluster features, providing a transferable mechanism for maintaining continuity under evolving streams.

admission.reason: The abstract clearly concerns one-pass short-text stream clustering with evolving cluster representations, episodic memory, and replay, but it does not say whether an incoming item can create a genuinely new cluster, whether forced attachment occurs, or whether merge/split/retirement decisions are supported. Admit to F4 only if the full method has explicit new-cluster creation or comparable novelty handling and evaluates assignment behavior under stream evolution.

title: Improving cross-document event coreference resolution by discourse coherence and structure
abstract: Proposes Event-oriented Cross-Document Coherence Enhancement to construct coherent textual context for event mentions that appear in different documents, then exploits rhetorical discourse structure to obtain global interaction information. The method is evaluated on ECB+ and GVC for clustering mentions of the same real-world event.

admission.reason: The method combines generated cross-document coherence with rhetorical discourse structure for same-event clustering, but this overlaps substantially with the admitted 2023 discourse-structure paper and other coherence candidates. The abstract does not show a uniquely important evidence ablation or identity-semantic contribution that warrants another reading slot. Identifier is UNCHECKED.

title: Resolving Event Coreference with Supervised Representation Learning and Clustering-Oriented Regularization
abstract: Learns representations of event mentions with clustering-oriented regularization and then forms event chains through agglomerative clustering. It evaluates both within- and cross-document event coreference on ECB+.

admission.reason: The paper is genuine cross-document event-coreference work, but the abstract emphasizes supervised representation learning, clustering-oriented regularization, and agglomerative clustering rather than evidence for deciding same versus different events, uncertainty, partial identity, or longitudinal correction. It therefore adds less to the open gaps than the admitted F1 candidates.
